question.text: If a trader expects the RBI to cut the repo rate at its next policy meeting, which GOI bond futures position would benefit?

answer.text: A simultaneous long and short in the same-tenor GOI bond futures (offsetting position)
Neither long nor short GOI bond futures would benefit

explanation.text: The Logic: An RBI rate cut pushes bond yields lower; lower yields mean higher bond prices; a long GOI bond futures position profits when bond prices rise (option A). NISM Series IV p.162 explicitly states that traders go long GOI bond futures when interest rates are expected to fall, and p.166 illustrates the same with a long-hedge example. The Trap: Option B is the wrong direction. Option C nets to zero exposure. Option D is contradicted by the source. In the original ambiguous version one of the distractors was "Short MIBOR futures", which was also source-supported: p.162 also says traders sell Overnight MIBOR futures when rates are expected to fall (because MIBOR futures are priced as 100 - rate, and the rate-fall makes the futures price rise, so the short loses; or alternatively the workbook frames Overnight MIBOR rate-as-price). The MIBOR distractor has been removed and the stem narrowed to GOI bond futures so that option A is uniquely correct. Note: The original question was ambiguous because p.162 supports both Long GOI bond futures AND Sell/Short Overnight MIBOR futures as positions that benefit from falling rates. The stem has been narrowed to "GOI bond futures positions" only, and the MIBOR distractor replaced, so option A is uniquely correct. Source: NISM Series IV, Dec 2025, pp.162, 166.
